examples.knowledge_point: Determining Intervals of Increasing or Decreasing Displacement
examples.problem: The displacement $s,$ in meters, relative to a fixed origin $O$ of a particle moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis is given by $s(t) = t^4 - 32t$, where $t \geq 0$ is the time measured in seconds. Determine the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x.$
examples.worked_solution:
If the particle moves in the direction of decreasing $x,$ then its velocity is negative. 

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4}-32t) \\  & =4{t}^{3}-32\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x$, we solve the inequality $v(t) <    0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & <0 \\ 4{t}^{3}-32 & <0 \\ 4{t}^{3} & <32 \\ {t}^{3} & <8 \\ t & <2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of decreasing $x$ is $t\in\left[ 0, 2\right).$

feedback.problem:
The position $s(t)$ of a particle (in meters) at time $t$ seconds is given by 

$$
s(t)={t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the time at which the particle is stationary.
feedback.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to calculate the velocity function. We can do that by taking the derivative of the position function, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t) \\  & =2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t+{t}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{t} \\  & =2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t \\  & =t(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t+1)\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m/s}.$ So, we set $v=0$ and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t+1) & =0 \\ 2\operatorname{ln}⁡t+1 & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡t & =-\frac{1}{2} \\ t & ={e}^{-1/2} \\ t & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary at $t=\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}\,\text{s}.$
